claim: Most of the components in the yeast secretory pathway have been studied, yet a high-resolution temporal timeline of their participation is lacking.
source: Most of the components in the yeast secretory pathway have been studied, yet a high-resolution temporal timeline of their participation is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: At the trans-Golgi network (TGN) Sec4's GEF, Sec2, is recruited to Ypt31-positive compartments, quickly followed by Sec4 and Myo2 and vesicle formation.
source: At the trans-Golgi network (TGN) Sec4's GEF, Sec2, is recruited to Ypt31-positive compartments, quickly followed by Sec4 and Myo2 and vesicle formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: While transported to the bud tip, the entire exocyst complex, including Sec3, is assembled on to the vesicle.
source: While transported to the bud tip, the entire exocyst complex, including Sec3, is assembled on to the vesicle.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of exocyst component localization during vesicle transport.

claim: Before fusion, vesicles tether for 5 s.
source: Before fusion, vesicles tether for 5 s, during which the vesicle retains the exocyst complex and stimulates lateral recruitment of Rho3 on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During tethering, the vesicle retains the exocyst complex and stimulates lateral recruitment of Rho3 on the plasma membrane.
source: Before fusion, vesicles tether for 5 s, during which the vesicle retains the exocyst complex and stimulates lateral recruitment of Rho3 on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of protein localization during the tethering phase.

claim: Sec2 and Myo2 are rapidly lost from vesicles during tethering.
source: Sec2 and Myo2 are rapidly lost, followed by recruitment of cytosolic Sro7, and finally the SM protein Sec1, which appears for just 2 s prior to fusion.
evidence: This is based on time-resolved imaging data showing the dynamics of these proteins.

claim: Sro7 is recruited to vesicles after Sec2 and Myo2 are lost.
source: Sec2 and Myo2 are rapidly lost, followed by recruitment of cytosolic Sro7, and finally the SM protein Sec1, which appears for just 2 s prior to fusion.
evidence: This temporal sequence is derived from experimental observations.

claim: The SM protein Sec1 appears for just 2 s prior to fusion.
source: Sec2 and Myo2 are rapidly lost, followed by recruitment of cytosolic Sro7, and finally the SM protein Sec1, which appears for just 2 s prior to fusion.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Many of the proteins involved in the secretory pathway were first identified and characterized in yeast.
source: Indeed, many of the proteins involved in the secretory pathway were first identified and characterized in yeast (Novick et al., 1980; Novick, 2014), which remains the organism in which the secretory pathway is best understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work in the field.

claim: Yeast remains the organism in which the secretory pathway is best understood.
source: Indeed, many of the proteins involved in the secretory pathway were first identified and characterized in yeast (Novick et al., 1980; Novick, 2014), which remains the organism in which the secretory pathway is best understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A similar timeline has been previously defined for the events and components of yeast endocytosis, a process which involves hundreds of copies of some proteins and takes on the order of 10–12 s.
source: A similar timeline has been previously defined for the events and components of yeast endocytosis, a process which involves hundreds of copies of some proteins and takes on the order of 10–12 s (Picco et al., 2015), but this work represents the first such timeline for exocytosis, the totality of which occurs over approximately 5 s.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This work represents the first such timeline for exocytosis, the totality of which occurs over approximately 5 s.
source: A similar timeline has been previously defined for the events and components of yeast endocytosis, a process which involves hundreds of copies of some proteins and takes on the order of 10–12 s (Picco et al., 2015), but this work represents the first such timeline for exocytosis, the totality of which occurs over approximately 5 s.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current work and is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Secretory vesicles are transported by the myosin-V motor protein, Myo2 along actin cables at about 3 µm/s.
source: Initial studies showed that secretory vesicles are transported by the myosin-V motor protein, Myo2 along actin cables at about 3 µm/s (Donovan and Bretscher, 2012; Donovan and Bretscher, 2015b; Santiago-Tirado et al., 2011; Schott et al., 1999; Schott et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sec4 is the Rab protein which associates with secretory vesicles and has a number of known effectors, including the exocyst, the myosin-V motor Myo2, and Sro7.
source: Of particular interest is the timing of effectors of Sec4, the Rab protein which associates with secretory vesicles and has a number of known effectors, including the exocyst, the myosin-V motor Myo2, and Sro7 (Guo et al., 1999; Jin et al., 2011; Rossi et al., 2018; Schott et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work identifying these interactions.

claim: At the TGN, a GTPase cascade results in the generation of secretory vesicles.
source: At the TGN, a GTPase cascade results in the generation of secretory vesicles (Novick, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Arf-GEF Sec7 activates Arf1, which in turn recruits Pik1-Frq1 (the phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase complex) and the TRAPPII Rab-GEF complex.
source: The Arf-GEF Sec7 activates Arf1, which in turn recruits Pik1-Frq1 (the phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase complex) and the TRAPPII Rab-GEF complex.
evidence: This describes a known biochemical cascade in the secretory pathway.

claim: TRAPPII recruits Ypt31/32 (Rab11 homologs), which recruits another Rab-GEF Sec2, which finally activates and recruits the secretory vesicle Rab, Sec4.
source: TRAPPII then recruits Ypt31/32 (Rab11 homologs), which recruits another Rab-GEF Sec2, which finally activates and recruits the secretory vesicle Rab, Sec4 (Thomas et al., 2019; Thomas and Fromme, 2016; Walch-Solimena et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ypt31/32 level has recently been shown to peak on compartments a full eight seconds after Sec7.
source: Ypt31/32 and Sec7 have frequently been used as interchangeable TGN markers; however, Ypt31/32 level has recently been shown to peak on compartments a full eight seconds after Sec7 (Highland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Endogenously tagged Sec7-mNeonGreen occasionally appears to fragment into small compartments or vesicles, but most Sec7 appears to dissipate around the time of fragmentation.
source: While endogenously tagged Sec7-mNeonGreen occasionally appears to fragment into small compartments or vesicles, most Sec7 appears to dissipate around the time of fragmentation, leaving resulting vesicles difficult to identify (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: mNeonGreen(mNG)-tagged Ypt31 can be followed through vesiculation and appears to remain on vesicles through fusion with the plasma membrane.
source: By contrast, mNeonGreen(mNG)-tagged Ypt31 can be followed through vesiculation and appears to remain on vesicles through fusion with the plasma membrane (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Sec2 appeared on the Ypt31-containing TGN approximately 2 s prior to separation.
source: Sec2 first appeared on the Ypt31-containing TGN approximately 2 s prior to separation, whereas Sec4 and the Myo2-marker appeared approximately 1 s before separation, and, presumably, about one second after Sec2 (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Sec4 and the Myo2-marker appeared approximately 1 s before separation from the TGN.
source: Sec2 first appeared on the Ypt31-containing TGN approximately 2 s prior to separation, whereas Sec4 and the Myo2-marker appeared approximately 1 s before separation, and, presumably, about one second after Sec2 (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The close temporal proximity of Sec4 and Myo2 arrival suggests that Myo2 is likely the first effector of Sec4 recruited to secretory vesicles.
source: The close temporal proximity of Sec4 and Myo2 arrival suggests that Myo2 is likely the first effector of Sec4 recruited to secretory vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal data presented.

claim: Myo2's early recruitment relative to other exocytic factors is probably aided by the fact that Myo2 is also a direct effector of Ypt31.
source: This early recruitment relative to other exocytic factors is probably aided by the fact that Myo2 is also a direct effector of Ypt31 (Lipatova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Only compartments marked with Sec2 or Sec4 appeared capable of moving diffusely for up to several seconds.
source: While Sec4, Sec2, and Myo2 were all found to be rapidly directed towards the bud following separation from the TGN—generally in under half a second—only compartments marked with Sec2 or Sec4 appeared capable of moving diffusely for up to several seconds, suggesting that at least some vesicles can separate from the TGN without first acquiring Myo2.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of vesicle movement.

claim: At least some vesicles can separate from the TGN without first acquiring Myo2.
source: While Sec4, Sec2, and Myo2 were all found to be rapidly directed towards the bud following separation from the TGN—generally in under half a second—only compartments marked with Sec2 or Sec4 appeared capable of moving diffusely for up to several seconds, suggesting that at least some vesicles can separate from the TGN without first acquiring Myo2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some vesicles move diffusely.

claim: The machinery driving secretory vesicle formation has not yet been identified.
source: It's remarkable that the machinery driving secretory vesicle formation has not yet been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of Vps1 results in cells containing larger compartments capable of maturing to the point that they recruit Sec4 and apparently fuse with the plasma membrane.
source: Loss of this small GTPase which is known to act at the endosome (Chi et al., 2014), results in cells containing larger compartments capable of maturing to the point that they recruit Sec4 and apparently fuse with the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in vps1∆ cells shown in a figure.

claim: Loss of Vps1 directly challenges the notion that the 80–100 nm vesicles themselves are essential for secretion.
source: This directly challenges the notion that the 80–100 nm vesicles themselves are essential for secretion, but will need to be examined more closely in future studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations in vps1∆ cells.

claim: Ypt31 and Ypt32 are often described interchangeably as they are considered functionally redundant.
source: Ypt31 and Ypt32 are often described interchangeably as they are considered functionally redundant (deletion of one or the other is consistent with viability, whereas loss of both is lethal).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ypt32 is more prominent on compartments within the bud compared to Ypt31.
source: Interestingly, while the relative recruitment timing of Sec2 and Sec4 was similar when compared to Ypt32 compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), relative Ypt32 to Ypt31 ratios appeared to mark subtly different compartments, with Ypt32 being more prominent on compartments within the bud (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The exocyst complex is comprised of single copies of Sec3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, Exo70, and Exo84.
source: The exocyst complex, comprised of single copies of Sec3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, Exo70, and Exo84, tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane before fusion and is primarily thought to localize to the vesicles themselves, ahead of membrane delivery (Boyd et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the exocyst complex, supported by a citation.

claim: The exocyst complex tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane before fusion.
source: The exocyst complex, comprised of single copies of Sec3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, Exo70, and Exo84, tethers secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane before fusion and is primarily thought to localize to the vesicles themselves, ahead of membrane delivery (Boyd et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the exocyst, supported by a citation.

claim: Sec3 has long been suggested to be a 'landmark' of secretory vesicle tethering—residing on the plasma membrane, apart from the other seven subunits of the complex on the vesicle itself.
source: Sec3, however, has long been suggested to be a 'landmark' of secretory vesicle tethering—residing on the plasma membrane, apart from the other seven subunits of the complex on the vesicle itself.
evidence: This describes a long-standing model in the field.

claim: The long-standing model suggests that once a vesicle comes into proximity of the plasma membrane, Sec3 then joins the bulk of the complex to complete the exocyst and facilitate tethering.
source: This long-standing model suggests that once a vesicle comes into proximity of the plasma membrane, Sec3 then joins the bulk of the complex to complete the exocyst and facilitate tethering (Finger et al., 1998; Wiederkehr et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes a model supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More recent studies suggest that the yeast exocyst complex is an obligatory heterooctamer, with Sec3 always being bound to the other components with no discernible subcomplexes.
source: More recent studies suggest that the yeast exocyst complex is an obligatory heterooctamer, with Sec3 always being bound to the other components with no discernible subcomplexes (Heider et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Each exocyst component, including Sec3, could be seen on vesicles in the mother cell, although clear vesicular localization was generally only noticeable in immediate proximity to the bud neck and within the bud itself.
source: In this study, each exocyst component, including Sec3, was individually tagged with mNeonGreen. When each component was imaged, they could be seen on vesicles in the mother cell, although clear vesicular localization was generally only noticeable in immediate proximity to the bud neck and within the bud itself (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Fluorescence loss of Sec3 and Sec5 from the bud during constant photobleaching of the mother cell was identical.
source: Additionally, fluorescence loss of Sec3 and Sec5 from the bud during constant photobleaching ('FLIP') of the mother cell was identical, suggesting that Sec3 recycles to the mother cell at the same rate as other exocyst components (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from a FLIP experiment shown in a figure.

claim: Sec3 recycles to the mother cell at the same rate as other exocyst components.
source: Additionally, fluorescence loss of Sec3 and Sec5 from the bud during constant photobleaching ('FLIP') of the mother cell was identical, suggesting that Sec3 recycles to the mother cell at the same rate as other exocyst components (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FLIP experiment data.

claim: Sec3 appears to be a component of the octameric exocyst complex in vivo which associates with secretory vesicles ahead of tethering and is not likely to be a spatial 'landmark' component of the exocyst.
source: Thus, Sec3 appears to be a component of the octameric exocyst complex in vivo which associates with secretory vesicles ahead of tethering and is not likely to be a spatial 'landmark' component of the exocyst. This echoes earlier work downplaying the landmark model of Sec3 function (Roumanie et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An average of 22 vesicles enter the bud per minute.
source: An average of 22 vesicles enter the bud per minute (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Secretory vesicles were found to tether for about five seconds before fusion with the plasma membrane.
source: In this study, secretory vesicles were found to tether for about five seconds before fusion with the plasma membrane; a far shorter time than previously believed.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Prior work had indicated a 'long' tether-to-fusion time for vesicles on the order of 15–18 s.
source: Prior work had indicated a 'long' tether-to-fusion time for vesicles on the order of 15–18 s (Alfaro et al., 2011; Donovan and Bretscher, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The presence of the GFP-tag on Sec4 itself affects Sec4 function.
source: Interestingly, we found early on in this study that the presence of the GFP-tag on Sec4 itself affects Sec4 function. A significant increase in tether-to-fusion time was seen when no untagged Sec4 was available (such as in a GFP-Sec4/GFP-Sec4 diploid or GFP-Sec4 haploid; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: GFP-Sec4 signal on the vesicle remains constant throughout the duration of tethering, only rapidly disappearing after several seconds.
source: By measuring the average intensity of GFP-Sec4 signal on tethered vesicles in the diploids, we found that GFP-Sec4 signal on the vesicle remains constant throughout the duration of tethering, only rapidly disappearing after several seconds, suggesting that Sec4 is not extracted from the vesicle during tethering (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity shown in a figure.

claim: Sec4 is not extracted from the vesicle during tethering.
source: By measuring the average intensity of GFP-Sec4 signal on tethered vesicles in the diploids, we found that GFP-Sec4 signal on the vesicle remains constant throughout the duration of tethering, only rapidly disappearing after several seconds, suggesting that Sec4 is not extracted from the vesicle during tethering (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence intensity data.

claim: Both Sec3-mNG and Sec15-mNG remain on tethered vesicles for about the same time as the tether-to-fusion time of GFP-Sec4.
source: Next, we determined the time that exocyst components Sec3-mNG and Sec15-mNG associate with tethered vesicles. Both Sec3-mNG and Sec15-mNG remain on tethered vesicles for about the same time as the tether-to-fusion time of GFP-Sec4, although both consistently appeared slightly shorter (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in a figure.

claim: At tethering hot-spots, secretory vesicles can be seen to tether sequentially and/or simultaneously.
source: During the current study, it became evident that a lower temporal resolution could result in longer apparent vesicle tethering due to a newly observed phenomenon of tethering 'hot-spots'. At these transient locations, secretory vesicles can be seen to tether sequentially (Figure 3A) and/or simultaneously (Figure 3B, Video 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures and videos.

claim: Disruption of actin cables with Latrunculin B resulted in an accumulation of secretory vesicles in the mother.
source: Disruption of actin cables with Latrunculin B resulted in an accumulation of secretory vesicles in the mother (Figure 3C) thereby precluding obtaining a definitive answer to the involvement of actin cables ends as hot-spots.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Disruption of actin cables caused a significant elongation of tethering-to-fusion time.
source: Moreover, this disruption caused a significant elongation of tethering-to-fusion time with individual tethering events being moderately easier to identify due to their more broad distribution within the bud (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Patches of Bni1 only persist for slightly longer than the lifetime of a single vesicle tethering event (mean, 6.4 s).
source: Interestingly, though puncta and patches of Bni1 (the formin within midsized buds responsible for actin cable assembly) only persist for slightly longer than the lifetime of a single vesicle tethering event (mean, 6.4 s), patches of another exocytic protein, Boi2, were capable of lasting significantly longer (median, 16.5 s; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Patches of Boi2 were capable of lasting significantly longer than Bni1 patches (median, 16.5 s).
source: Interestingly, though puncta and patches of Bni1 (the formin within midsized buds responsible for actin cable assembly) only persist for slightly longer than the lifetime of a single vesicle tethering event (mean, 6.4 s), patches of another exocytic protein, Boi2, were capable of lasting significantly longer (median, 16.5 s; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Many, but not all, vesicles appear to tether at Boi2-mNG puncta.
source: We previously showed that Rho3 primarily localizes to the plasma membrane, and not on internal vesicles, with concentration on the membrane increasing toward the bud tip and transient discrete puncta of yet higher concentration (Gingras et al., 2020). Imaging of Exocyst-3x-mScarlet with endogenous expression of this previously developed Rho3-imNG showed that Rho3 initially concentrates in puncta at vesicles shortly following their arrival to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Sec4 GTP-hydrolysis, as promoted by the genetically redundant Rab-GAPs Msb3 and Msb4, is believed to be important for maintaining proper tether-to-fusion time.
source: Sec4 GTP-hydrolysis, as promoted by the genetically redundant Rab-GAPs Msb3 and Msb4, is believed to be important for maintaining proper tether-to-fusion time (Donovan and Bretscher, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Homozygous deletion of msb4 with heterozygous deletion of msb3 leads to a modest but significant increase in tether-to-fusion time.
source: Homozygous deletion of msb4 with heterozygous deletion of msb3 (msb3∆/MSB3 msb4∆/msb4∆) leads to a modest but significant increase in tether-to-fusion time, while the opposite (msb3∆/msb3∆ msb4∆/MSB4) results in much greater increase in tether-to-fusion time.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Replacement of one copy of Sec4 in a diploid with the constitutively active Sec4(Q79L) allele results in a similar effect on tethering as msb3 deletion.
source: A similar effect on tethering can be seen when one copy of Sec4 in a diploid is replaced with the constitutively active Sec4(Q79L) allele (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Excess active Sec4 is seen on the plasma membrane of msb3∆/msb3∆ cells.
source: Excess active Sec4 is seen on the plasma membrane of msb3∆/msb3∆ cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: There was no difference in vesicle tether-to-fusion time with expression of the constitutively active, plasma membrane-bound Sec4.
source: Notably, there was no difference in vesicle tether-to-fusion time with expression of the constitutively active, plasma membrane-bound Sec4 (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Delayed hydrolysis of vesicle-bound Sec4-GTP elongates tethering time.
source: Thus, delayed hydrolysis of vesicle-bound Sec4-GTP elongates tethering time.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Heterozygous deletion of Gdi1 also had no significant effect on secretory vesicle tether-to-fusion time despite also resulting in accumulated Sec4 on the plasma membrane.
source: Limitation of GDI availability by heterozygous deletion of Gdi1 also had no significant effect on vesicle tether-to-fusion time despite also resulting in accumulated Sec4 on the plasma membrane (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The fact that Sec4 can be retained on the plasma membrane by Gdi1 limitation strongly supports that the rapid loss of Sec4 signal from a tethered vesicle is representative of fusion.
source: In addition to further supporting the conclusion that accumulated Sec4 on the plasma membrane does not interfere or elongate tether-to-fusion time, the fact that Sec4 can be retained in this way strongly supports that the rapid loss of Sec4 signal from a tethered vesicle is representative of fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Sec2 and Smy1 appear to dissociate from secretory vesicles shortly after tethering.
source: Unlike Sec4 and the exocyst complex, Sec2 and Smy1 appear to dissociate from secretory vesicles shortly after tethering (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Sec2 is the first protein observed to depart the vesicle, with Sec2-mNG puncta lasting on average 2.8 s after becoming stationary at the plasma membrane.
source: Sec2 is the first protein observed to depart the vesicle, with Sec2-mNG puncta lasting on average 2.8 s after becoming stationary at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Smy1 only remains associated with the vesicle for an average of 3 s after tethering.
source: Smy1, which associates with vesicle-bound Myo2 and resides on vesicles through transport (Lillie and Brown, 1994; Lillie and Brown, 1992; Lwin et al., 2016), only remains associated with the vesicle for an average of 3 s after tethering.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: Sro7 does not localize directly to vesicles and instead appears in short-lived puncta at the plasma membrane.
source: Three additional exocytic components, Sro7, Mso1, and Sec1, were found to exclusively localize to puncta at the plasma membrane. Sro7 is a nonessential protein involved in polarity maintenance and secretion that directly binds and regulates the soluble SNAP-25 homolog, Sec9 (Hattendorf et al., 2007; Lehman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The median longevity of Sro7 puncta was approximately 3.4 s (mean, 3.8 s).
source: The median longevity of Sro7 puncta was approximately 3.4 s (mean, 3.8 s; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: None of the Sro7 signal appeared to localize to diffusive or actively transported secretory vesicles, whether in the mother or bud.
source: None of the Sro7 signal appeared to localize to diffusive or actively transported secretory vesicles, whether in the mother or bud.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Disruption of vesicle tethering by a sec6-4 mutation induced broad Sro7-mNG localization across the plasma membrane.
source: Additionally, disruption of vesicle tethering by a sec6-4 mutation induced broad Sro7-mNG localization across the plasma membrane (Figure 5C), perhaps due to its known association with the exocytic SNARE Sec9.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Sec1 puncta longevity had a median time of 2.1 s (mean, 2.3 s).
source: Here, we visualized Sec1-mNG (Figure 5E, Video 4) and found the shortest localization timing of any exocytic component examined, with Sec1 puncta longevity having a median time of 2.1 s (mean, 2.3 s; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Unlike Sro7, Sec1 arrival and departure times were different, with the accumulation of signal taking slightly longer than its dissipation following peak intensity.
source: Interestingly, unlike Sro7, Sec1 arrival and departure times were different, with the accumulation of signal taking slightly longer than its dissipation following peak intensity (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of fluorescence intensity over time shown in a figure.

claim: Mso1 was found to have a similarly short lifetime to Sec1, not significantly different from Sec1 (median 2.5 s, mean 2.6 s).
source: Mso1, a small nonessential protein tightly associated with Sec1 and suggested to be an effector of Sec4, was found to have a similarly short lifetime, not significantly different from Sec1 (median 2.5 s, mean 2.6 s; Figure 5A; Weber et al., 2010; Weber-Boyvat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure, supported by citations.

claim: About 23±9 molecules of Sec2 could be seen on vesicles during transport.
source: About 23±9 molecules of Sec2 could be seen on vesicles during transport.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Few copies of Sro7 (20±8) and Sec1 (14±5) were found to localize to their respective membrane puncta in the bud.
source: Finally, few copies of Sro7 (20±8) and Sec1 (14±5) were found to localize to their respective membrane puncta in the bud.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: Sec4 and the exocyst depart from exocytic sites around the same time.
source: However, even in this strain we can see that Sec4 and the exocyst depart from exocytic sites around the same time (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Myo2 begins dissociating shortly after the start of tethering.
source: Further, since several components (Sec2, Myo2, Smy1, and the exocyst itself) are transported to the tethering site on the vesicle, alignment of loss of these components to the moment of tethering is easy, for example tracking the loss of a Tomato-Myo2-marker compared to GFP-Sec4, confirms that Myo2 begins dissociating shortly after the start of tethering (Figure 6B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Rho3 on the plasma membrane concentrates briefly after Exocyst-3x-mScarlet vesicle tethering.
source: Rho3 was visualized with a recently developed internal-mNG (imNG) tag and compared to the arrival of vesicles marked by Exocyst-3x-mScarlet (Figure 6C; Gingras et al., 2020). Alignment of multiple such events illustrates that Rho3 peaks at sites of tethered vesicles about 1.5 s after tethering (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Rho3 peaks at sites of tethered vesicles about 1.5 s after tethering.
source: Alignment of multiple such events illustrates that Rho3 peaks at sites of tethered vesicles about 1.5 s after tethering (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Sro7 signal peaked between 3 and 4 s after tethering.
source: When Sro7-mNG was imaged alongside Exocyst-3x-mScarlet, Sro7 signal peaked between 3 and 4 s after tethering (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Approximately 20% of Sro7-mNG puncta did not colocalize with clear exocyst puncta.
source: Interestingly, while Sro7 almost always co-localized with clear exocyst puncta in still images (as expected by the timing of its arrival relative to tethering), approximately 20% of Sro7-mNG puncta did not colocalize (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Peak Sec1 intensity corresponded with the moment of exocyst loss, the expected moment of vesicle fusion.
source: Alignment of several Sec1 puncta co-imaged with Exocyst-3x-mScarlet showed that peak Sec1 intensity corresponded with the moment of exocyst loss, the expected moment of vesicle fusion (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Smy1 arrived and began decreasing in intensity approximately 5 s before Sec1 peak.
source: When the timing of this Sec1-mNG peak was compared to Smy1-mScarlet, we found that Smy1 arrived and began decreasing in intensity (like Myo2 in Figure 6B) approximately 5 s before Sec1 peak, indirectly illustrating the time between vesicle arrival and fusion (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Loss of the plasma membrane SNAREs Sso2 or heterozygous reduction in the functionally redundant Sso1 resulted in a longer tethering time.
source: Loss of the plasma membrane SNAREs Sso2 or heterozygous reduction in the functionally redundant Sso1, resulted in a longer tethering time, as did the heterozygous reduction of Sec9.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Heterozygous reduction of Sec9 resulted in a longer tethering time.
source: Loss of the plasma membrane SNAREs Sso2 or heterozygous reduction in the functionally redundant Sso1, resulted in a longer tethering time, as did the heterozygous reduction of Sec9.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Heterozygous reduction in the vesicle SNARE Snc2 had little effect on tethering time.
source: Heterozygous reduction in the vesicle SNARE Snc2, which is functionally redundant with Snc1, had little effect (homozygous loss of Snc2 results in vesicle accumulation which precluded measurement of tethering time).
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Over-expression of either Snc2, Sec9, or Sso2 had a consistently minor, but not significant, effect of lowering tether-to-fusion time.
source: While SNARE limitation had a clear detrimental effect on tether-to-fusion time, over-expression of either Snc2, Sec9, or Sso2 had a consistently minor, but not significant, effect of lowering tether-to-fusion time (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Overexpression of Sec2, Msb3 (or heterozygous deletion of Sec2) has no significant effect on secretory vesicle tether-to-fusion time.
source: Next, we examined proteins that regulate the level of active Sec4, the vesicle-bound Rab GEF Sec2, and the plasma membrane bound Rab GAP Msb3. While Msb3 deletion was shown to elongate vesicle tethering time (see Figure 4A), its overexpression had no such clear effect. Neither did overexpression nor heterozygous reduction of Sec2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: In msb3∆/msb3∆ cells, the rapid release of Sec2 from secretory vesicles after tethering is unchanged, whereas loss of Myo2 and the exocyst is delayed and the duration of Sro7 and Sec1 is extended.
source: This reveals that the rapid release of Sec2 from secretory vesicles after tethering is unchanged, whereas loss of Myo2 and the exocyst is delayed and the duration of Sro7 and Sec1 is extended (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Rho3 had no significant effect on tether-to-fusion time when either overexpressed or heterozygously deleted.
source: Rho3, which likely plays an important role in the initial establishment of tethering, also had no significant effect on tether-to-fusion time when either overexpressed or heterozygously deleted (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: When Rho3 was overexpressed ectopic vesicle tethering could occasionally be observed within the mother.
source: Despite this, when Rho3 was overexpressed ectopic vesicle tethering could occasionally be observed within the mother (Figure 7E, inset), though these tethering events were largely non-productive.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Deletion of both copies of Sro7 showed no significant effect on vesicle tethering time.
source: Consistent with its non-essentiality, deletion of both copies of Sro7 showed no significant effect on vesicle tethering time (Figure 7F), whereas overexpression of Sro7 via a 2µ plasmid, resulted in a significant elongation of vesicle tethering time.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Overexpression of Sro7 resulted in a significant elongation of vesicle tethering time.
source: Consistent with its non-essentiality, deletion of both copies of Sro7 showed no significant effect on vesicle tethering time (Figure 7F), whereas overexpression of Sro7 via a 2µ plasmid, resulted in a significant elongation of vesicle tethering time.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The only protein for which overexpression resulted in a statistically significant lower vesicle tether-to-fusion time was Myo2.
source: Notably, under the stringent statistical tests required for the many comparisons made in this study, the only protein for which overexpression resulted in a statistically significant lower vesicle tether-to-fusion time was Myo2.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Loss of actin cables lengthens tethering times.
source: Together with the observation that loss of actin cables lengthens tethering times (Figure 3C), this result suggests that F-actin and Myo2 participate in the establishment of productive tethering (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Overexpression of Sec1 resulted in a slightly elongated tether-to-fusion time.
source: Overexpression of Sec1 resulted in a slightly elongated tether-to-fusion time (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Heterozygous deletion of Sec1 had no clear effect on tether-to-fusion time.
source: Heterozygous deletion of Sec1 had no clear effect on tether-to-fusion time.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of Mso1 had no measurable effect on tether-to-fusion time.
source: Unsurprisingly, overexpression of the nonessential Mso1 protein also had no measurable effect, however, a strain lacking this same protein exhibited one of the largest observed increases in tether-to-fusion time (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: A strain lacking Mso1 exhibited one of the largest observed increases in tether-to-fusion time.
source: Unsurprisingly, overexpression of the nonessential Mso1 protein also had no measurable effect, however, a strain lacking this same protein exhibited one of the largest observed increases in tether-to-fusion time (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Sec1-mNG puncta have similar longevity to wildtype in mso1∆ cells.
source: When we examined the longevity of Sec1-mNG in an mso1 null, we saw no such change in the time from Sec1 punctum appearance to disappearance (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: There were no apparent changes in the number of Sec1 molecules per punctum in the mso1 null strain.
source: Nor were there any apparent changes in the number of Sec1 molecules per punctum in the mso1 null strain (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Broad plasma membrane localization of Sec1 was diminished in the mso1∆ strain, especially for cells with midsized buds.
source: We did, however, find that broad plasma membrane localization of Sec1 (outside of discrete puncta) was diminished in the mso1∆ strain, especially for cells with midsized buds, in which vesicle tethering times were normally measured (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in a figure.

claim: Mso1's primary function may be to increase the local concentration of Sec1 on the plasma membrane near sites of polarized growth, hastening its ultimate recruitment to a tethered vesicle thereby promoting efficient secretory vesicle fusion.
source: These data suggest that Mso1s primary function may be to increase the local concentration of Sec1 on the plasma membrane near sites of polarized growth, hastening its ultimate recruitment to a tethered vesicle thereby promoting efficient secretory vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Sec1 has a positively charged C-terminus, and Mso1 has an amphipathic N-terminus, either of which when visualized independently localize broadly to the plasma membrane.
source: This is further supported by our new observations concerning Sec1 membrane recruitment. Sec1 has a positively charged C-terminus, and Mso1 has an amphipathic N-terminus (Figure 8F), either of which when visualized independently localize broadly to the plasma membrane (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Simultaneous loss of the Mso1 N-terminus and the Sec1 C-terminus is lethal.
source: Individual loss of either of these regions from Sec1 or Mso1, can be tolerated, but simultaneous loss of these two membrane-associating regions is lethal (Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from tetrad dissections shown in figures.

claim: The extended Sec1 tail is unique to fungi and all Sec1 C-termini appear to contain this highly positively charged sequence.
source: It is interesting to note that the extended Sec1 tail is unique to fungi and all Sec1 C-termini appear to contain this highly positively charged sequence, although the length of the preceding linker region varies (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Mso1 is unique to fungi, specifically ascomycetes, but is considerably more variable between species, with the Sec1-binding domain being the principal highly-conserved motif within the protein sequence.
source: Mso1 is also unique to fungi, specifically ascomycetes, but is considerably more variable between species, with the Sec1-binding domain being the principal highly-conserved motif within the protein sequence (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in a figure.
